content: Bronchiectasis is a chronic respiratory condition characterized by permanent and abnormal widening and distortion of the smaller airways. This structural damage often leads to bacterial colonization, which in turn causes persistent coughing, sputum production, breathlessness, and further airway damage. Long-term use of macrolide antibiotics has been proposed as a therapeutic strategy to suppress bacterial infections and reduce inflammation. This approach may result in fewer exacerbations, reduced symptoms, improved lung function, and enhanced quality of life. However, more evidence is needed to evaluate the effectiveness of macrolides in eradicating specific bacterial pathogens and to assess the extent of antibiotic resistance associated with their use. The objective of this study was to assess the impact of macrolide antibiotics in treating adults and children with bronchiectasis. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) lasting at least four weeks were included, comparing macrolides with either placebo or no intervention in patients with stable bronchiectasis. Participants were diagnosed using bronchography, plain chest radiographs, or high-resolution computed tomography. Studies involving patients who had recently received continuous or high-dose antibiotics, or those with conditions such as cystic fibrosis, sarcoidosis, or allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, were excluded. The primary outcomes assessed were exacerbation frequency, hospitalizations, and serious adverse events. The review included 15 trials (14 parallel-group RCTs and one cross-over RCT) with intervention durations ranging from 8 weeks to 24 months. Eleven studies involved 690 adults, while four studies included 190 children. Among the adult studies, six used azithromycin, four used roxithromycin, and one used erythromycin. The pediatric studies used azithromycin, clarithromycin, erythromycin, or roxithromycin. Nine adult studies compared macrolides with placebo, and two compared macrolides with no intervention. In children, one study compared macrolides with placebo, and another compared macrolides with no intervention. In adults, macrolides significantly reduced the frequency of exacerbations compared to placebo (odds ratio [OR] 0.34, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.22 to 0.54; moderate-quality evidence). This corresponds to a number needed to treat (NNT) of 4 (95% CI 3 to 8). However, no significant difference in exacerbation frequency was observed between macrolides and no intervention (OR 0.31, 95% CI 0.08 to 1.15; moderate-quality evidence). Macrolides were also associated with improved quality of life compared to placebo (mean difference [MD] -8.90, 95% CI -13.13 to -4.67; moderate-quality evidence). There was no evidence of a reduction in hospitalizations (OR 0.56, 95% CI 0.19 to 1.62; low-quality evidence), serious adverse events (OR 0.49, 95% CI 0.20 to 1.23; low-quality evidence), or adverse events (OR 0.83, 95% CI 0.51 to 1.35) in adults treated with macrolides compared to placebo. In children, macrolides reduced exacerbation frequency more effectively than placebo (incidence rate ratio [IRR] 0.50, 95% CI 0.35 to 0.71; low-quality evidence). However, no significant differences were observed in hospitalizations (OR 0.28, 95% CI 0.07 to 1.11; low-quality evidence), serious adverse events (OR 0.43, 95% CI 0.17 to 1.05; low-quality evidence), or adverse events (OR 0.78, 95% CI 0.33 to 1.83) between macrolides and placebo in children. Importantly, macrolide use in children was associated with a significant increase in macrolide-resistant bacteria (OR 7.13, 95% CI 2.13 to 23.79), including resistance to Streptococcus pneumoniae (OR 13.20, 95% CI 1.61 to 108.19) and Staphylococcus aureus (OR 4.16, 95% CI 1.06 to 16.32). Quality of life outcomes were not reported in the pediatric studies. In conclusion, long-term macrolide therapy may reduce exacerbation frequency and improve quality of life, particularly in adults with bronchiectasis. However, the evidence is primarily derived from studies on azithromycin and is limited in children. Caution is warranted due to the potential for increased microbial resistance and the known risks of cardiovascular death and other serious adverse events associated with macrolides in other populations. Further research is needed to clarify these risks in patients with bronchiectasis.
